```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = TRUE,          
  eval = TRUE,

  warning = FALSE,      
  error = FALSE         
)

# Core Libraries
library(readxl)
library(tidyverse)
library(scales)
library(knitr)
library(skimr)

# Shared Global Color Palette
primary_color   <- "#104E8B"
secondary_color <- "#E69F00"

```

# 1. Introduction

Customer churn is one of the most critical business metrics for
subscription-based services, directly impacting long-term revenue and
customer lifetime value. While introductory analyses typically focus on
basic demographic splits and broad service adoption rates, understanding
the nuanced drivers of attrition requires a deeper, multi-dimensional
investigation. Building upon the foundational concepts introduced during
the lecture using the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, this assignment
aims to conduct an independent exploratory data analysis (EDA) in R.
This analysis focuses on relationships specifically investigating the
interplay between dempgraphic customer segment, complex billing
mechanisms, contract flexibility, tech support utilization, and customer
tenure. By defining our own analytical questions, we seek to uncover
hidden behavioral patterns and risk indicators that can inform more
targeted retention strategies.

# 2. Dataset

This empirical study utilizes the IBM Telco Customer Churn dataset, a
benchmark repository comprising $7,043$ individual customer records and
$33$ structural features. The dataset encompasses four primary
dimensions of consumer profile data: demographic attributes (such as
gender, senior status, and household dependents), account and billing
mechanics (including subscription tenure, contract type, payment method,
monthly expenditures, and cumulative charges), specific
telecommunication service subscriptions (such as multi-line telephony
and digital streaming), and auxiliary internet security add-ons
(including online backup, device protection, and technical support). The
primary target variable, `Churn`, is a binary indicator denoting whether
a subscriber terminated their services within the observed timeframe.
Consistent with typical telecommunication retail sectors, the dataset
exhibits moderate class imbalance, wherein approximately $26.5\%$ of the
customer base accounts for attrition events, establishing a robust
foundation for investigating multi-variate behavioral patterns and risk
factors associated with customer retention.

The dataset in use is sourced from Kaggle and the link below: **Telco
customer churn: IBM dataset**

<https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/yeanzc/telco-customer-churn-ibm-dataset>

For the analysis we used the file `Telco_customer_churn.xlsx`.

# 3. Data Inspection

First, loading the dataset from the .xlsx file, it should be placed it
in the same directory as this R Markdown file, or should be adapted the
file path below.

```{r load-data}
customers <- read_excel(
  "Telco_customer_churn.xlsx",
  sheet = "Telco_Churn"
)
```

Inspecting the dimensions, variable names, data types and initial
records.

```{r inspect-data}

nrow(customers)   # Number of observations
ncol(customers)   # Number of variables

str(customers)    # Shows the structure of the dataset, including variable types and example values

```

Counting the variables according to their imported data types,
distinguishing numeric columns from categorical columns. This provides
an initial overview of the dataset structure.

```{r imported-data-type}

# Identify column types as imported
is_numeric <- vapply(customers, is.numeric, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))
is_categorical <- vapply(customers, is.character, FUN.VALUE = logical(1))

imported_type_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable_type = c("Numeric", "Categorical", "Other"),
  Number_of_variables = c(
    sum(is_numeric),
    sum(is_categorical),
    sum(!is_numeric & !is_categorical)
  )
)

imported_type_summary

```

Storage types do not always correspond to analytical roles, in fact ZIP
codes and binary outcomes as Churn Value are stored as numbers. We
therefore review variable meanings before selecting descriptive
statistics and visualizations.

Let's see the first ten rows of the dataset to have a first look on it.

```{r first-rows}

head(customers,10) 
```

# 4. Data Quality

Before exploring customer characteristics and their relationships with
churn, we assess data quality by checking for duplicated rows and
missing values. These checks help us identify potential issues and
decide whether data preparation is required. Missing values are
evaluated according to their meaning rather than automatically removing
all incomplete records.

### 4.1 Duplicates

We check for completely duplicated rows by comparing all columns. If
duplicates are found, repeated occurrences are removed while retaining
the first occurrence. This check concerns identical records, not
repeated customer identifiers with potentially different information.

```{r duplicates}

customers_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(customers))

if (customers_duplicates > 0) {
  customers <- customers[!duplicated(customers), ]
  cat(customers_duplicates, "duplicated row(s) removed.")
} else {
  cat("No duplicated rows found. No rows were removed.")
}
  
```

### 4.2 Missing values

We count missing values in each variable and calculate their percentage
relative to the total number of customers. The resulting table is sorted
in descending order of missing-value count to highlight the most
affected variables. This provides an initial overview, but the
appropriate treatment depends on why the information is missing.

```{r missing-values}

customers_na <- colSums(is.na(customers))

na_analysis <- tibble(
  Variable = names(customers),
  Missing_values = customers_na,
  Missing_values_percentage = customers_na / nrow(customers) * 100
)

cat("Variable(s) with missing values:", paste0(names(customers[customers_na > 0]), collapse = ", "))

na_analysis <- na_analysis |> arrange(desc(Missing_values))
na_analysis
```

We investigate missing values in **Total Charge**s and **Churn Reason**
separately because they have different meanings. Missing total charges
may relate to newly established customer relationships, whereas a
missing churn reason may be expected when a customer has not left the
company.

```{r missing-values-Total-Charges}

customers[is.na(customers["Total Charges"]), 
          c("CustomerID", "Total Charges", "Tenure Months", "Churn Value", "Churn Label")]

```

The 11 customers with missing total charges all have zero months of
tenure and are recorded as retained customers. This pattern is
consistent with newly established customer relationships for which
cumulative charges may not yet be available. However, it does not
provide sufficient justification to replace the missing values with
zero.

We retain these customers in the dataset because information required
for other analyses, including their churn outcome, is available. For
calculations involving Total Charges, we exclude missing values only
from the relevant calculation and report the number of valid
observations. Removing these customers entirely would also change the
sample used for churn comparisons.

We examine missing **churn reasons** separately for retained and churned
customers. For each group, we calculate the number of customers, the
number of missing reasons and the percentage of missing reasons within
that group. This distinguishes expected missingness from potentially
incomplete information about customers who left.

```{r missing-values-Churn-Reason}

customers %>%
  group_by(`Churn Label`) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Missing_reason = sum(is.na(`Churn Reason`)),
    Missing_reason_percentage = sum(is.na(`Churn Reason`)) / n() * 100
  )
```

All 5,174 retained customers have a missing churn reason, while all
1,869 churned customers have a recorded reason. Missingness in this
variable is therefore structural: customers who remained with the
company do not have a reason for leaving.

We do not impute these values or remove the corresponding customers.
Analyses of churn reasons will be restricted to customers who churned,
while retained customers will remain included in the other analyses.

### 4.3 Identification of variable with zero variance (columns with the same value in all the rows)

Let's identify all the variable with the same value in all observations,
those variables are not interesting in terms of statistical analysis, so
we won't analyse them.

```{r zero-variance-vars}

single_value_cols <- customers %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ n_distinct(.) == 1)) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Single_Value") %>%
  filter(Single_Value == TRUE)

print(single_value_cols)

```

### 4.4 Validation of the target and visualization

`Churn Value` is used for calculations: 1 means churned and 0 means
retained. `Churn Label` represents the same outcome in text "Yes" and
"No".

```{r target-validation}

# Check missing values and valid target categories
stopifnot(
  !anyNA(customers$`Churn Label`),
  !anyNA(customers$`Churn Value`),
  all(customers$`Churn Label` %in% c("No", "Yes")),
  all(customers$`Churn Value` %in% c(0, 1))
)

# Display the correspondence between the two representations
target_check <- table(
  Churn_label = customers$`Churn Label`,
  Churn_value = customers$`Churn Value`
)

target_check
```

We summarize the target distribution using customer percentages. This
establishes the overall observed churn rate and provides a reference for
subsequent comparisons between customer segments.

```{r target-visualization}

target_summary <- customers |>
  ungroup() |>
  count(`Churn Label`, name = "Customers") |>
  mutate(
    Percentage = 100 * Customers / sum(Customers)
  )

plot_churn <- ggplot(target_summary, aes( x = factor(`Churn Label`, levels = c("Yes", "No")), y = Percentage)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#104E8B", color = "#27445D", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6,) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      label = sprintf(
        "%.1f%%",
        Percentage,
        format(Customers, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
      )
    ),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Value Distribution (%)",
    subtitle = "Univariate Analysis of Churn Label",
    x = "Churned",
    y = "Customers (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
    theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5), 
  )

plot_churn
```

The chart shows that 26.5% of customers churned, whereas 73.5% remained
with the company. Retained customers therefore represent the majority
class. This overall churn rate provides a reference for subsequent
segment-level comparisons: a segment with a higher rate would exhibit
above-average observed churn.

# 5. Univariate Analysis

Univariate analysis examines each variable individually. We will isolate
categorical variables to study their frequencies (via bar charts) and
numerical variables to analyze their distribution (via histograms).
Please note that we will exclude any previously identified zero-variance
variables from this analysis, as well as the 'Customer ID' column since
it serves as the dataset's unique key.

```{r univariate-vars}

customers_univ <- customers %>% 
  select(-CustomerID, -Count, -Country, -State)

# Summary with skim function of the dataset select for univariate analysis. Divided in categorical and numerical variables

skim(customers_univ)

```

### 5.2 Demographic customers analysis

We describe gender, senior status, partner status and dependent status.
These distributions show how common each customer characteristic is;
they do not yet describe its association with churn. Dependents are not
necessarily children: they can include other dependent household
members.

```{r demographic-vars, fig.width= 10, fig.height = 8}

demographic_long <- customers_univ %>% 
  select(Gender, `Senior Citizen`, Partner, Dependents) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% 
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = c("Gender", "Senior Citizen", "Partner", "Dependents")))

plot_demographic <- ggplot(demographic_long, aes(x = Value, y = after_stat(prop), group = Variable, fill = Value)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count", fill = "#104E8B", color = "#27445D", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    stat = "count", 
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", after_stat(prop) * 100)), 
    vjust = -0.5, 
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x") + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Demographic Distribution (%)",
    subtitle = "Univariate Percentage Analysis of Gender, Senior Citizen, Partner, and Dependents",
    y = "Percentage of Total Customers",
    x = ""
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5), 
  )

plot_demographic
```

The demographic panels describe the composition of the customer base
rather than differences in churn risk. Female customers account for
49.5% of the sample. Senior citizens represent 16.2%, while 48.3% report
having a partner and 76.9% report having dependents. Each panel uses the
full customer sample as its denominator, allowing the relative size of
the categories to be compared within that demographic characteristic.

### 5.3 Tech services and subscriptions analysis

We describe all the variables related to tech services and
subscriptions, showing their distribution.

```{r services-vars, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 12}
services_long <- customers_univ %>% 
  select(`Phone Service`, `Multiple Lines`, `Internet Service`, `Online Security`, 
         `Online Backup`, `Device Protection`, `Tech Support`, `Streaming TV`, `Streaming Movies`) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% 
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = c(
    "Phone Service", "Multiple Lines", "Internet Service", "Online Security", 
    "Online Backup", "Device Protection", "Tech Support", "Streaming TV", "Streaming Movies"
  )))

plot_services <- ggplot(services_long, aes(x = Value, y = after_stat(prop), group = Variable, fill = Value)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "count", fill = "#104E8B", color = "#27445D", alpha = 0.8, width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    stat = "count", 
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f%%", after_stat(prop) * 100)),     vjust = -0.5, 
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) + 
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0,1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Services and Subscriptions Distribution (%)",
    subtitle = "Univariate Percentage Analysis",
    y = "Percentage of Total Customers",
    x = ""
  ) +
 theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )

plot_services
```

Phone service is subscribed to by 90.3% of customers. The
internet-service panel separates fiber-optic, DSL and no-internet
customers, while the remaining panels describe the adoption of
additional services. The distinction between "No" and "No internet
service" is essential: the former indicates that the customer does not
subscribe to the specific add-on, whereas the latter indicates that the
underlying internet service is absent. Likewise, "No phone service" in
the Multiple Lines panel should not be interpreted as a decision to
reject an additional telephone line. The percentages shown are
calculated across all customers.

### 5.5 Billing Profile Analysis

Now, the description of the billing profile through distribution

```{r billing-vars-cat, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8}

billing_long <- customers_univ %>% 
  select(`Paperless Billing`, `Payment Method`) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>%

  ) +

    y = "Percentage of Total Customers",
```

The payment-method panel describes the relative prevalence of electronic
checks, mailed checks, automatic bank transfers and automatic

Electronic checks should not be grouped with automatic payments merely

characterize billing arrangements, not payment reliability, customer
satisfaction or churn risk.

### 5.6 Numeric variables univariate analysis

Continuous numerical indicators require a distinct analytical
methodology compared to categorical attributes. Instead of counting
discrete frequencies, we utilize histograms to observe density
distribution, skewness, modality, and data sparsity across our
quantitative dimensions: customer subscription life cycle duration
(`Tenure Months`), monthly overhead rates (`Monthly Charges`),
cumulative financial commitments (`Total Charges`), and corporate equity
valuations (`CLTV`).

Two strategic adjustments have been applied to this quantitative
framework:

1.  **Explicit Units of Measurement**: Because individual variables
    follow entirely different ranges the global axis title is removed,
    specific units (Months, \$) are integrated directly into the panel
    titles.

2.  **Data Discretization (`bins = 30`)**: A uniform structure of 30
    bins is selected to balance granularity and readability, capturing
    distribution shapes without introducing random visual noise. The
    parameter `na.rm = TRUE` safely manages the 11 unestablished
    accounts within `Total Charges` without crashing the global
    visualization.

```{r numeric-vars, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 18}

numeric_vars <- customers_univ %>% 
  select(`Tenure Months`, `Monthly Charges`, `Total Charges`, CLTV)

summary(numeric_vars)

numeric_long <- customers_univ %>% 
  select( 
    "Tenure (Months)" = `Tenure Months`, 
    "Monthly Charges ($)" = `Monthly Charges`, 
    "Total Charges ($)" = `Total Charges`, 
    "Customer Lifetime Value" = CLTV
  ) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Value") %>% 
  mutate(Variable = factor(Variable, levels = c(
    "Tenure (Months)", "Monthly Charges ($)", "Total Charges ($)", "Customer Lifetime Value"
  )))

plot_numeric <- ggplot(numeric_long, aes(x = Value)) +
  geom_histogram(fill = "#104E8B", color = "#222222", alpha = 0.8, bins = 30, na.rm = TRUE) +
  facet_wrap(~ Variable, scales = "free", ncol = 1) + 
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Numeric Variables",
    subtitle = "Univariate Analysis of Tenure Months, Monthly Charges, Total Charges and CLTV",
    x = "",
    y = "Frequency (Count)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12), 
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5), 
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#EAEAEA")
  )

plot_numeric
```

The histograms describe four different quantitative dimensions, the
vertical axis reports customer counts, not probability density.

- Tenure Months measures the duration of the customer relationship. Its
  median is 29 months, with an interquartile range from 9 to 55 months.
  This distribution provides context for distinguishing recently
  acquired customers from customers with longer relationships.

- Monthly Charges describes recurring customer expenditure. The median
  monthly charge is 70.35\$.

- Total Charges measures accumulated charges rather than recurring
  expenditure. Its median is 1397.5\$ missing observations are omitted
  from this histogram only; the corresponding customers are retained for
  other analyses.

- CLTV denotes customer lifetime value. The median recorded CLTV is
  4527.

# 6. Multivariate Analysis

Having established the univariate distributions of demographic, billing,
and services characteristics, we now transition to multivariate
relationships. Specifically, we investigate how demographic (seniority
and household segments), contract types, transactional friction (payment
methods), and technical support and security add-ons interact to
influence customer churn.

Rather than relying on simple bivariate correlations, we examine
conditional probabilities and cross-tabulations to uncover underlying
risk profiles.

### 6.1 Senior status and churn

**Question:** Does observed churn differ between senior and non-senior
customers, and does this difference remain within contract types?

```{r senior-churn}

senior_churn <- customers %>% 
  group_by(`Senior Citizen`) %>% 
  mutate(`Senior Citizen` = factor(`Senior Citizen`, levels = c("Yes", "No"))) %>% 
  summarise(
    Customers = n(), 
    Churned = sum(`Churn Value`), 
    Churn_rate = 100 * sum(`Churn Value`) / Customers
  )

ggplot(senior_churn, aes(x = `Senior Citizen`, y = Churn_rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#104E8B", color = "#222222", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_rate, 1), "%")),
    vjust = -0.5, 
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("Yes" = "Senior", "No" = "Non-senior")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(title = "Churn by Senior Status", x = "", y = "Churn rate (%)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )
```

The chart shows a clear difference in observed churn between senior and
non-senior customers. The churn rate is 41.7% among senior customers,
compared with 23.6% among non-senior customers, a difference of 18.1
percentage points. In relative terms, the observed churn rate among
seniors is approximately 1.77 times that of non-seniors. Because the
bars represent churn percentages within each group rather than absolute
customer counts, the comparison accounts for differences in group size.
The results indicate that senior customers have a higher observed
propensity to leave in this dataset.

```{r senior-contract}

# Calculate churn rates by contract type and senior status
senior_contract_churn <- customers %>%
  group_by(Contract, `Senior Citizen`) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Churned = sum(`Churn Value`),
    Churn_rate = sum(`Churn Value`) / Customers * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Compare senior and non-senior churn within each contract type
ggplot(senior_contract_churn, aes(x = Contract, y = Churn_rate, fill = `Senior Citizen`)) +
  geom_col(color = "#222222", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_rate, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5, 
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("No" = "#104E8B", "Yes" = "#E69F00"),
    labels = c("No" = "Non-senior", "Yes" = "Senior")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 70)) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn by Contract Type and Senior Status",
    x = "Contract type",
    y = "Churn rate (%)",
    fill = "Customer group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )
```

The chart shows that observed churn varies by both contract type and
senior status. Month-to-month customers have the highest churn rates in
both groups: 54.6% among seniors and 39.6% among non-seniors. Churn is
lower among customers with one-year contracts, at 15.3% and 10.7%,
respectively, and lowest among those with two-year contracts, at 4.1%
and 2.7%.

Senior customers exhibit higher observed churn within every contract
category. However, the absolute gap between senior and non-senior
customers is largest for month-to-month contracts, at approximately 15.1
percentage points, compared with 4.6 points for one-year contracts and
1.4 points for two-year contracts. The senior–non-senior difference
therefore remains visible after separating customers by contract type,
although its magnitude varies across categories. Overall, senior
customers on month-to-month contracts form the segment with the highest
observed churn rate among the six groups examined.

### 6.2 Partner and dependent status

**Question:** How does churn vary across the four combinations of
partner and dependent status?

```{r household-churn}

# Calculate churn rates for the four household-status combinations
household_churn <- customers %>%
  group_by(Partner, Dependents) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Churned = sum(`Churn Value`),
    Churn_rate = sum(`Churn Value`) / Customers * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(household_churn, aes(x = Partner, y = Churn_rate, fill = Dependents)) +
  geom_col(color = "#222222", position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_rate, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(labels = c("No" = "No partner", "Yes" = "Partner")) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("No" = "#104E8B", "Yes" = "#E69F00"),
    labels = c("No" = "No dependents", "Yes" = "Dependents")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 50)) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn by Partner and Dependent Status",
    x = "Partner status",
    y = "Churn rate (%)",
    fill = "Dependent status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )
```

Observed churn varies considerably across the four combinations of
partner and dependent status. Customers with neither a partner nor
dependents have the highest churn rate, at 34.4%, followed by customers
with a partner but no dependents, at 29.5%. Customers with dependents
but no partner have a lower churn rate of 16.6%, while those with both a
partner and dependents have the lowest rate, at 4.2%.

The chart shows that having dependents is associated with lower observed
churn both among customers with a partner and among those without one.
However, the groups differ in size: the no-partner/with-dependents group
contains only 302 customers, compared with 3,339 in the
no-partner/no-dependents group.

```{r household-contract}

# Define household profiles using partner and dependent status
household_contract_churn <- customers %>%
  mutate(
    Household = case_when(
      Partner == "No"  & Dependents == "No"  ~ "No partner / No dependents",
      Partner == "No"  & Dependents == "Yes" ~ "No partner / Dependents",
      Partner == "Yes" & Dependents == "No"  ~ "Partner / No dependents",
      Partner == "Yes" & Dependents == "Yes" ~ "Partner / Dependents"
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(Household, Contract) %>%
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Churned = sum(`Churn Value`),
    Churn_rate = sum(`Churn Value`) / Customers * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(household_contract_churn, aes(x = Contract, y = Household, fill = Churn_rate)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_rate, 1), "%\n", "n = ", Customers)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = c("Month-to-month", "One year", "Two year")) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = c(
    "Partner / Dependents", "Partner / No dependents", 
    "No partner / Dependents", "No partner / No dependents"
  )) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F7FBFF", high = "#104E8B", limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn by Household Profile and Contract Type",
    subtitle = "Each cell shows the churn rate and group size",
    x = "Contract type",
    y = "Household profile",
    fill = "Churn rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank()
  )
```

The heatmap shows that observed churn varies across both household
profiles and contract types. Month-to-month contracts have the highest
churn rate within every household profile. Among month-to-month
customers, churn is highest for those with a partner but no dependents
(51.9%), followed by those with neither a partner nor dependents
(46.2%). The corresponding rates are lower for customers with
dependents: 26.5% without a partner and 12.5% with a partner.

Separating customers by contract type adds an important qualification to
the earlier household-level comparison. Although customers with neither
a partner nor dependents had the highest overall churn rate, customers
with a partner but no dependents have the highest rate within each
contract category. This highlights the importance of considering
contract composition when interpreting differences between household
profiles. No churn events are recorded among customers with dependents
on one-year or two-year contracts. These zero rates describe the
observed sample and should not be interpreted as evidence of zero
underlying churn risk, particularly for the smaller groups.

### 6.3 Senior status, household profile, internet services and churn

```{r demographic-service}

# Data cleaning & feature engineering
telco_analysis <- customers |> 
  mutate(
    # Recode Age indicator
   Age_Group = if_else(`Senior Citizen` == "Yes", "Senior", "Non-Senior"),
    
    # Recode Household Structure
    Household = case_when(
      Partner == "Yes" & Dependents == "Yes" ~ "Partner / Dependents",
      Partner == "Yes" & Dependents == "No"  ~ "Partner / No dependents",
      Partner == "No"  & Dependents == "Yes" ~ "No partner / Dependents",
      Partner == "No"  & Dependents == "No"  ~ "No partner / No dependents"
    ),
    
    # Count of Value-Added Add-on Services (0 to 6)
    Addon_Services_Count = (`Online Security` == "Yes") + (`Online Backup` == "Yes") + 
                           (`Device Protection` == "Yes") + (`Tech Support` == "Yes") + 
                           (`Streaming TV` == "Yes") + (`Streaming Movies` == "Yes")
  )
```

The statistical test is a mathematical procedure used to determine
whether there is sufficient evidence in sample data to reject a null
hypothesis (H₀), which assumes that there is no effect, relationship, or
difference in the population.

Hypothesis ($H_0$): Internet service type adoption is independent of
customer age group.

```{r age-internet}

# TEST A: Chi-Square Test of Independence (Age Group vs Internet Service)
chisq_age_internet <- chisq.test(table(telco_analysis$Age_Group, telco_analysis$`Internet Service`))
print(chisq_age_internet)

age_internet_table <- table(
  telco_analysis$Age_Group,
  telco_analysis$`Internet Service`
)

# Calculate percentages within each senior-status group
age_internet_pct <- as.data.frame(
  round(prop.table(age_internet_table, margin = 1) * 100, 1)
)
names(age_internet_pct) <- c("Age_Group", "Internet_Service", "Percentage")
age_internet_table

age_internet_pct
```

Pearson’s chi-squared test indicates a statistically significant
association between senior status and internet service type, X-squared =
495.80, p-value \< 2.2 e-16. The null hypothesis of independence is
therefore rejected.

Within-group percentages show that 72.8% of senior customers subscribe
to fiber-optic internet, compared with 38.4% of non-senior customers.
Senior customers have lower proportions of DSL subscriptions (22.7%
versus 36.6%) and no internet service (4.6% versus 25.0%). These results
indicate that the two groups differ substantially in their internet
subscription profiles.

This analysis provides useful context for subsequent churn comparisons:
differences in internet service composition should be considered when
examining the higher overall churn observed among senior customers.

```{r age-internet-plot}

ggplot(
  age_internet_pct,
  aes(
    x = Internet_Service,
    y = Percentage,
    fill = Age_Group
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    color = "#222222",
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Percentage, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = c("DSL", "Fiber optic", "No")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c("Non-Senior" = "#104E8B", "Senior" = "#E69F00"),
    labels = c("Non-Senior" = "Non-senior", "Senior" = "Senior")
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
  labs(
    title = "Internet Service Distribution by Senior Status",
    subtitle = "Percentages calculated within each senior-status group",
    x = "Internet service",
    y = "Percentage of customers (%)",
    fill = "Customer group"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()+
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )


```

```{r senior-internet-churn}
# Compare churn by senior status and internet service
senior_internet_churn <- customers |>
  group_by(`Senior Citizen`, `Internet Service`) |>
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Churn_rate = mean(`Churn Value`) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

senior_internet_churn
```

The table compares observed churn rates between senior and non-senior
customers within each internet-service category. Senior customers have a
higher churn rate than non-senior customers in all three
internet-service groups. The difference is largest among DSL customers,
where the churn rate is 30.1% for seniors compared with 17.6% for
non-seniors, a difference of approximately 12.5 percentage points.
Fiber-optic customers have the highest observed churn rate in both
groups: 47.3% among seniors and 39.9% among non-seniors. Customers
without internet service have the lowest churn rates, at 9.6% among
seniors and 7.3% among non-seniors. The senior/no-internet group
contains only 52 customers and five churn events, so its percentage
should be interpreted with caution. These results suggest that the
higher overall churn observed among senior customers persists after
separating customers by internet-service type.

Hypothesis ($H_0$): The distribution of the number of value-added add-on
services is the same across the four household profiles.

```{r household-addons}

# TEST B: Test whether the distribution of add-on services differs across household profiles
kruskal_household_addons <- kruskal.test(
  Addon_Services_Count ~ Household,
  data = telco_analysis
)
kruskal_household_addons

household_addons_summary <- telco_analysis |>
  group_by(Household) |>
  summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Mean_Addons = mean(Addon_Services_Count),
    Median_Addons = median(Addon_Services_Count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

household_addons_summary
```

```{r household-addons-plot}

blue_palette <- c(
  "No partner / Dependents"      = "#BDD7E7",
  "No partner / No dependents"   = "#6BAED6",
  "Partner / Dependents"         = "#3182BD",
  "Partner / No dependents"      = "#08519C"
)

# Display the distribution of add-on services by household profile
ggplot(
  telco_analysis,
  aes(x = Household, y = Addon_Services_Count, fill = Household)
) +
  geom_boxplot(
    outlier.shape = 21,
    outlier.size = 1.5,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  stat_summary(
    fun = mean,
    geom = "point",
    shape = 18,
    size = 3,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
    limits = c(
      "No partner / Dependents",
      "No partner / No dependents",
      "Partner / Dependents",
      "Partner / No dependents"
    )
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = blue_palette) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    breaks = 0:6,
    limits = c(-0.5, 6.5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Number of Value-Added Add-on Services by Household Profile",
    subtitle = "Diamonds indicate group means; boxes show the median and interquartile range",
    x = "Household profile",
    y = "Number of add-on services"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
    
```

The Kruskal-Wallis test indicates that the distribution of the number of
value-added add-on services differs across household profiles,
H(3)=358.02, p\<2.2e-16. The null hypothesis of identical distributions
is therefore rejected.

Customers with a partner but no dependents have the highest mean number
of add-on services, at 2.65, while customers without a partner but with
dependents have the lowest mean, at 1.46. Customers with both a partner
and dependents have an intermediate mean of 2.09, whereas customers with
neither a partner nor dependents average 1.69 add-on services. The
boxplot shows the full distribution of the add-on count within each
household profile, including medians and variability.

```{r}
# Calculate churn rate by household profile and number of add-on services
household_addon_churn <- telco_analysis |>
  dplyr::group_by(Household, Addon_Services_Count) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    Customers = n(),
    Churn_rate = mean(`Churn Value`) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# Plot churn by add-on count for each household profile
ggplot(

) +
```

The line chart shows that observed churn generally decreases as the
number of subscribed value-added add-on services increases within each
household profile. For example, among customers with a partner but no
dependents, the churn rate falls from 53.8% among customers with one
add-on to 6.9% among those with six add-ons. Customers with both a
partner and dependents have the lowest churn rates across most add-on
levels. However, some categories contain few customers, so their
percentages should be interpreted with caution.

### 6.4 Effect of Value-Added Services on Churn

Exploring how services—categorized into Security & Support Services
(Online Security, Online Backup, Device Protection, Tech Support) and
Entertainment Services (Streaming TV, Streaming Movies) acts as a
retention anchor and influences average monthly spending.

```{r services-influence}
telco_addons <- customers %>%
  mutate(
    Security_Support_Count = (`Online Security` == "Yes") + (`Online Backup` == "Yes") + 
                             (`Device Protection` == "Yes") + (`Tech Support` == "Yes"),
    Entertainment_Count = (`Streaming TV` == "Yes") + (`Streaming Movies` == "Yes"),
    Total_Addons = Security_Support_Count + Entertainment_Count,
    
    # Create service tier buckets
 Service_Tier = case_when(
      `Internet Service` == "No" ~ "No Internet",
      Total_Addons == 0          ~ "Basic (0 Add-ons)",
      Total_Addons <= 2          ~ "Moderate (1-2 Add-ons)",
      TRUE                       ~ "High (3+ Add-ons)"
    )
  )
```

Hypothesis ($H_0$): Customer churn rate is independent of the number of
value-added services bundled into the contract.

```{r services-test-1}

# TEST A: Chi-Square Test of Independence (Service Tier vs. Churn)
chisq_tier_churn <- chisq.test(table(telco_addons$Service_Tier, telco_addons$`Churn Label`))
print(chisq_tier_churn)

```

Hypothesis ($H_0$): Security and technical support services do not have
a statistically significant protective effect against churn compared to
entertainment add-ons.

```{r services-test-2}

# TEST B: Logistic Regression to evaluate individual impact of each Add-on Service
logistic_model <- glm(
  `Churn Label` == "Yes" ~ `Online Security` + `Online Backup` + `Device Protection` + 
                           `Tech Support` + `Streaming TV` + `Streaming Movies` + `Monthly Charges`,
  data = telco_addons %>% filter(`Internet Service` != "No"),
  family = binomial
)
summary(logistic_model)

```

```{r services-test-3}

# Summary Table: Churn and Billing Metrics by Add-on Service Tier
addon_summary <- telco_addons %>%
  group_by(Service_Tier) %>%
  summarise(
    Customer_Count = n(),
    Avg_Monthly_Charges = mean(`Monthly Charges`),
    Avg_Tenure_Months = mean(`Tenure Months`),
    Churn_Rate_Pct = mean(`Churn Label` == "Yes") * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(addon_summary, caption = "Add-On Tier Performance Summary")
```

```{r services-plot}

# Figure 1: Churn Rate by Add-On Service Tier
fig_1 <- ggplot(telco_addons, aes(x = Service_Tier, fill = `Churn Label`)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = secondary_color, "Yes" = primary_color)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "top"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Churn Rate Across Value-Added Service Tiers",
    subtitle = "Analysis of churn risk as customers subscribe to additional services",
    x = "Service Bundle Complexity Tier",
    y = "Proportion of Customers",
    fill = "Churned"
  )

# Figure 2: Impact of Specific Add-On Services on Churn Probability
addon_proportions <- telco_addons %>%
  filter(`Internet Service` != "No") %>%
  select(
    `Churn Label`, `Online Security`, `Online Backup`, 
    `Device Protection`, `Tech Support`, `Streaming TV`, `Streaming Movies`
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(cols = -`Churn Label`, names_to = "Service", values_to = "Status") %>%
  filter(Status != "No internet service") %>%
  group_by(Service, Status) %>%
  summarise(
    Total = n(),
    Churned = sum(`Churn Label` == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE),
    Churn_Rate = (Churned / Total) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

print(fig_1)

fig_2 <- ggplot(addon_proportions, aes(x = reorder(Service, Churn_Rate), y = Churn_Rate, fill = Status)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", alpha = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = primary_color, "Yes" = secondary_color)) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "top"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Rate Comparison per Specific Value-Added Service",
    subtitle = "Comparing churn rates between subscribers ('Yes') and non-subscribers ('No')",
    x = "Value-Added Service",
    y = "Churn Rate (%)",
    fill = "Subscribed to Service"
  )

print(fig_2)
```

Customers with basic internet and zero add-ons exhibit the highest churn
rate approximately 40%, whereas customers subscribing to 3 or more
add-on services show a dramatic reduction in churn (under 15%).
TechSupport and OnlineSecurity provide the strongest individual
protective effects against cancellation. Non-subscribers to technical
support churn at more than double the rate of subscribers. While
streaming services (StreamingTV and StreamingMovies) increase monthly
charges, they do not reduce churn as effectively when standalone.
Security and support services act as foundational "anchors" that lock in
customer loyalty by increasing switching costs.

### 6.5 Technical support and churn by internet service type

High-cost services often carry higher baseline churn risk due to
customer sensitivity to pricing and service expectations. We investigate
whether auxiliary digital security and technical support add-ons can
mitigate this risk for different internet service.

```{r fiber-support-summary}

fiber_analysis <- customers %>%
  filter(`Internet Service` != "No") %>%
  group_by(`Internet Service`, `Tech Support`) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Customers = n(),
    Churn_Rate = (sum(`Churn Value`) / Total_Customers) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

ggplot(fiber_analysis, aes(x = `Tech Support`, y = Churn_Rate, fill = `Internet Service`)) +
  geom_col(
    color = "#222222",
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
    ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_Rate, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("DSL" = "#104E8B", "Fiber optic" = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Rate by Internet Service and Tech Support",
    x = "Tech Support Subscription",
    y = "Churn Rate (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )
```

The results highlight a clear pattern: customers subscribing to
technical support experience significantly lower attrition rates
compared to those without support. Providing proactive technical
infrastructure acts as a vital retention buffer for high-value accounts.

### 6.6 Contract Type, Payment Method, and Attrition

We first examine how structural contract flexibility and billing
mechanisms jointly affect customer retention. Month-to-month contracts
lack lock-in commitments, while electronic check payment methods
introduce transactional touchpoints that may increase friction. We
cross-tabulate contract types and payment methods against the churn
outcome.

```{r contract-payment-churn}

contract_payment_summary <- customers %>%
  group_by(Contract, `Payment Method`) %>%
  summarise(
    Total_Customers = n(),
    Churned_Customers = sum(`Churn Value`),
    Churn_Rate = (Churned_Customers / Total_Customers) * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  arrange(desc(Churn_Rate))

kable(contract_payment_summary, caption = "Churn Rate by Contract and Payment Method")
```

The statistical summary reveals that churn is heavily concentrated among
customers on month-to-month contracts using electronic check payment
methods, whereas customers on two-year contracts exhibit minimal
attrition regardless of billing mechanism.

To visualize this multi-variable relationship clearly without cluttering
proportions, we construct a faceted bar chart showing churn rates across
payment methods, split by contract length.

```{r contract-payment-plot}
ggplot(contract_payment_summary, aes(x = `Payment Method`, y = Churn_Rate, fill = Contract)) +
  geom_col(
    color = "#222222",
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = paste0(round(Churn_Rate, 1), "%")),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Month-to-month" = "#4292C6",
      "One year" = "#2171B5",
      "Two year" = "#08519C")     
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Churn Rate by Payment Method and Contract Type",
    x = "Payment Method",
    y = "Churn Rate (%)",
    fill = "Contract Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "top",
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "lines"),
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "#DCDCDC", fill = NA, size = 0.5)
  )

```

The visualization demonstrates that electronic check users on
month-to-month contracts experience churn rates exceeding 40%, whereas
long-term contract structures successfully insulate the firm against
payment-method-induced attrition.

### 6.7 Payment Methods and Electronic Invoicing

Explore whether customers using automatic payments (bank transfer/credit
card) have lower churn compared to those who pay via electronic check.

```{r payment-and-billing-influence}
# Categorize Payment Channels into Automatic vs. Manual
telco_payments <- customers %>%
  mutate(
    Payment_Type = if_else(
      grepl("automatic", `Payment Method`, ignore.case = TRUE),
      "Automatic Payment",
      "Manual Payment"
    ),
    PaymentMethod_Clean = case_when(
      `Payment Method` == "Electronic check" ~ "Electronic Check",
      `Payment Method` == "Mailed check" ~ "Mailed Check",
      `Payment Method` == "Bank transfer (automatic)" ~ "Bank Transfer (Auto)",
      `Payment Method` == "Credit card (automatic)" ~ "Credit Card (Auto)"
    )
  )
```

Hypothesis ($H_0$): Customer churn is independent of the payment channel
selected.

```{r payment-and-billing-test-1}

# TEST A: Chi-Square Test of Independence (Payment Method vs. Churn)
chisq_payment_churn <- chisq.test(table(telco_payments$PaymentMethod_Clean, telco_payments$`Churn Label`))
print(chisq_payment_churn)

```

Hypothesis ($H_0$): Adopting paperless billing (PaperlessBilling =
"Yes") has no significant association with customer attrition rates.

```{r payment-and-billing-test-2}

# TEST B: Chi-Square Test of Independence (Paperless Billing vs. Churn)
chisq_paperless_churn <- chisq.test(table(telco_payments$`Paperless Billing`, telco_payments$`Churn Label`))
print(chisq_paperless_churn)

# Test C: Wilcoxon Rank-Sum Test (Monthly Charges across Automatic vs. Manual Payments)
wilcox_charges_payment <- wilcox.test(`Monthly Charges` ~ Payment_Type, data = telco_payments)
print(wilcox_charges_payment)

# Summary Table: Churn and Billing Metrics by Payment Method and Invoicing Choice
payment_summary <- telco_payments %>%
  group_by(PaymentMethod_Clean, `Paperless Billing`) %>%
  summarise(
    Customer_Count = n(),
    Avg_Monthly_Charges = mean(`Monthly Charges`),
    Avg_Tenure_Months = mean(`Tenure Months`),
    Churn_Rate_Pct = mean(`Churn Label` == "Yes") * 100,
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(payment_summary, caption = "Payment Summary Metrics")
```

```{r payment-and-billing-plot}

# Figure 1: Churn Rate by Payment Method and Paperless Invoicing
figA <- ggplot(telco_payments, aes(x = PaymentMethod_Clean, fill = `Churn Label`)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", alpha = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ `Paperless Billing`, labeller = labeller(`Paperless Billing` = c("No" = "Paper Invoicing", "Yes" = "Paperless Invoicing"))) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = secondary_color, "Yes" = primary_color)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "top"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 5: Churn Rate Across Payment Methods and Invoicing Types",
    subtitle = "Comparing Electronic and Paperless options against traditional billing",
    x = "Payment Method",
    y = "Proportion of Customers",
    fill = "Churned"
  )

print(figA)

# Figure: Monthly Charges vs. Tenure by Payment Automation Type
figB <- ggplot(telco_payments, aes(x = `Tenure Months`, y = `Monthly Charges`, color = Payment_Type)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, size = 1.2) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, size = 1.2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Automatic Payment" = secondary_color, "Manual Payment" = primary_color)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    legend.position = "top"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Figure 6: Spending Trajectory and Tenure by Payment Automation",
    subtitle = "Evaluating how automatic payment adoption correlates with long-term retention",
    x = "Tenure (Months)",
    y = "Monthly Charges ($)",
    color = "Payment Channel Type"
  )

print(figB)
```

Customers paying via Electronic Check exhibit an exceptionally high
churn rate approximately 45%, significantly outperforming all other
payment channels in attrition risk. Electronic billing increases price
visibility and invoice awareness, prompting price-sensitive customers to
evaluate alternative competitors when rates fluctuate.

### 6.8 Tenure Milestones and Customer Lifetime Value

Finally, we examine how customer tenure influences estimated Customer
Lifetime Value (CLTV) across churned versus retained customers.
Understanding how financial value accumulates over time helps management
identify critical retention milestones during the customer lifecycle.

```{r tenure-cltv-summary}

tenure_cltv_summary <- customers %>%
  group_by(`Churn Label`) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Tenure = mean(`Tenure Months`),
    Mean_CLTV = mean(CLTV, na.rm = TRUE),
    Total_Customers = n(),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

kable(tenure_cltv_summary, caption = "Tenure and CLTV Summary")

ggplot(customers, aes(x = `Tenure Months`, y = CLTV, color = `Churn Label`)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 1.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("No" = primary_color, "Yes" = secondary_color)) +
  labs(
    title = "Customer Lifetime Value vs. Tenure Months by Churn Status",
    x = "Tenure Months",
    y = "Estimated CLTV",
    color = "Churned"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

The scatter plot demonstrates that retained customers generally achieve
longer tenure spans and cluster at higher lifetime values, whereas
churned customers predominantly exit early in their subscription
lifecycle when cumulative value and engagement are low.

# 7. Findings and Company Suggestions

### 7.1 Main findings

The analysis shows that customer churn is not evenly distributed across
customer segments. Overall, 26.5% of customers churned, while 73.5%
remained with the company. This overall rate provides the reference
against which the segment-level results should be interpreted.

Senior customers have a higher observed churn rate than non-senior
customers: 41.7% compared with 23.6%. This difference remains visible
within every contract type, although its size varies. The largest gap
occurs among month-to-month customers, where senior customers churn at
54.6% and non-senior customers at 39.6%. These results indicate that
senior status is associated with higher observed churn, but they do not
establish that senior status causes customers to leave.

Contract type is strongly associated with observed churn. Month-to-month
customers show the highest churn rates across household profiles and
senior-status groups, whereas customers with two-year contracts show the
lowest rates. This pattern is consistent with the idea that longer
contractual commitments are associated with greater customer retention,
although the observational nature of the data does not allow a causal
conclusion.

Household composition also matters. Customers with both a partner and
dependents have the lowest observed churn rate, at 4.2%, while customers
with neither a partner nor dependents have the highest rate, at 34.4%.
However, when household profiles are examined jointly with contract
type, customers with a partner but no dependents show the highest churn
rate within each contract category. This shows that the relationship
between household characteristics and churn should not be interpreted
using aggregate percentages alone.

Internet service type is another relevant dimension. Senior customers
are more likely than non-senior customers to subscribe to fiber-optic
internet, while non-senior customers are more likely to have DSL or no
internet service. Fiber-optic customers have the highest observed churn
rate within both senior-status groups. Therefore, the higher overall
churn among senior customers should be interpreted alongside their
different service composition.

### 7.2 Service adoption and churn

The number of subscribed add-on services is associated with observed
churn. Among internet customers, those with no add-on services have the
highest churn rate, while customers with three or more add-ons have a
lower observed rate. Technical support is associated with a particularly
large difference: among fiber-optic customers, the churn rate is 49.4%
without technical support and 22.6% with technical support. A similar
pattern appears among DSL customers.

These findings suggest that security and support services may be
relevant to retention, but the analysis does not prove that subscribing
to an add-on causes customers to remain. Customers who choose these
services may also differ in contract type, tenure, monthly charges or
overall engagement. The relationship between add-on adoption and churn
should therefore be treated as exploratory.

### 7.3 Billing and payment patterns

Churn is concentrated among customers on month-to-month contracts who
pay by electronic check. This group has an observed churn rate of 53.7%,
the highest among the contract and payment-method combinations examined.
By contrast, customers on two-year contracts show low churn rates across
payment methods.

Paperless billing is also associated with higher observed churn within
each payment-method category. However, this association does not
demonstrate that electronic invoicing causes customers to leave. It may
reflect differences in customer profiles, contract types, tenure or
payment preferences. The results identify electronic-check customers on
month-to-month contracts as a segment that deserves further
investigation, rather than proving that paperless billing itself is a
churn driver.

### 7.4 Tenure and customer value

Retained customers have a longer average tenure than churned customers:
37.6 months compared with 18.0 months. They also have a higher average
recorded CLTV, at 4,490.9 compared with 4,149.4. These results are
consistent with the idea that customers who remain longer accumulate
more value over time.

However, the analysis does not establish the direction of this
relationship. Customers may churn early because they have not yet
developed a long relationship with the company, or early churn may
simply reduce the time available for value accumulation. The results
should therefore be interpreted as descriptive rather than causal.

### 7.5 Company suggestions

The findings suggest several areas for further investigation and
targeted retention activity.

First, month-to-month customers who pay by electronic check represent
the segment with the highest observed churn rate. The company should
investigate their service experience, billing preferences and contract
renewal behaviour before designing an intervention. Encouraging a move
toward automatic payment methods may be worth testing, but its effect on
retention should be evaluated through a controlled pilot rather than
assumed from this observational analysis.

Second, senior customers on month-to-month contracts are a high-priority
segment. They combine higher observed churn with shorter contractual
commitments. The company should examine whether their needs differ in
terms of service reliability, billing clarity or technical assistance,
rather than assuming that age alone explains their churn.

Third, technical support and security-related add-ons appear associated
with lower observed churn, particularly among fiber-optic customers. A
practical next step would be to test whether offering technical support
during the early months of a fiber-optic subscription improves
retention. Any such initiative should be evaluated against a comparison
group.

Finally, the company should avoid treating the observed associations as
proof of causation. The analysis identifies customer segments and
service patterns associated with higher or lower churn, but further
modelling, customer feedback and controlled experiments would be needed
to understand why customers leave and which retention actions are
effective.
